questions.short_title: Fatigue common a year after cardiac arrest
questions.question: At 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, which symptom was most common among survivors?
options: Anxiety
Depression
Insomnia
Fatigue
questions.explanation: Fatigue was reported by 35.8% of survivors, ahead of anxiety at 22.6% and depression at 18.0%, and it exceeded population norms. Keep in mind symptoms were self-reported and about a third of eligible survivors were lost to follow-up.

questions.short_title: Shorter pulse checks linked to more ROSC
questions.question: In the CaPTuRe study, how did pulse checks lasting 5 seconds or less compare with checks lasting 6-10 seconds?
options: They showed no difference in ROSC but shorter ETCO2 recovery times
They only benefited patients whose arrest was witnessed
They were linked to a higher ROSC rate (36.3% vs 19.5%) and better ETCO2 dynamics
They were linked to lower ROSC because interruptions were judged too brief to assess circulation
questions.explanation: Shorter checks were associated with roughly double the ROSC rate and more favourable ETCO2 loss and recovery patterns. The study was quasi-randomised, so healthier arrests may simply have had quicker checks, and the finding is hypothesis-generating.

questions.short_title: Infant carry slings rarely linked to OHCA
questions.question: In this registry review of cardiac arrests in children under two, which circumstance was most commonly documented surrounding the arrest?
options: Feeding during transport
Being found unresponsive in a cot, bed, sofa or pushchair
Infant carry sling use
Co-sleeping
questions.explanation: Co-sleeping featured in 33.3% of cases, ahead of children found unresponsive at 26.3%, while carry slings were linked to just 2 of 162 arrests. The single-region sample and free-text review mean this can't rule out a rare sling risk.

questions.short_title: Paediatric deterioration in the field poorly defined
questions.question: What gap did the scoping review find across all 28 studies of paediatric out-of-hospital deterioration?
options: Lack of a standard operational definition
Lack of any vital sign measurement
Lack of data from high-income countries
Lack of studies on children under 18
questions.explanation: No study offered an operational or standardised definition of deterioration, which limits comparability and consistent recognition of sick kids. As a scoping review it maps the field rather than pooling effects, and most included studies were retrospective.

questions.short_title: Who doesn't call an ambulance for chest pain
questions.question: Which group had higher odds of calling an ambulance for acute coronary syndrome than people living with others?
options: People living alone
Men
Adults under 49
People born outside Australia
questions.explanation: Living alone was linked to up to 48% higher odds of EMS use — the one equity factor pointing the other way. The review used vote-counting on heterogeneous observational studies, so treat all these figures as hypothesis-generating rather than precise effects.

questions.short_title: Cluster trials read differently to individual ones
questions.question: In prehospital, emergency and critical care trials, how did cluster-randomised trials compare with individually randomised ones?
options: Similar mortality, smaller length-of-stay effects
Smaller effects on every outcome measured
Similar effects on every outcome measured
They showed bigger mortality benefits
questions.explanation: Mortality effect estimates were much the same between the two trial types, but cluster trials reported significantly smaller effect sizes for length-of-stay or days-alive outcomes. The comparison was observational across heterogeneous meta-analyses, with under half reporting randomisation type, so treat it as context only.

questions.short_title: How ambulance models shape end-of-life care
questions.question: Across all three ambulance service models studied, how did paramedics mostly develop their end-of-life care skills?
options: Learning on the job
From university-based palliative care modules
Through mandatory annual end-of-life care training
Through an in-service specialist palliative care team
questions.explanation: In every case, learning on the job dominated, alongside limited access to records, anticipatory medicines and palliative advice. The innovative models improved resources, but structured training was still lacking.

questions.short_title: Why rural stroke care lags: system drivers
questions.question: According to this qualitative study, when did rural and coastal distance become most inequity-producing in prehospital stroke care?
options: When the patient lived alone or had subtle or atypical symptoms
When the nearest stroke unit lacked a pre-alert pathway
When combined with limited mobility, complex extrication or Category 2 demand
When crews had no consistent access to translation services
questions.explanation: Stakeholders described distance compounding delay only when it interacted with system pressures like limited patient mobility, complex extrication and Category 2 queueing. The findings come from providers only — no patients or carers were interviewed, and it reflects a single region.
